column11: three factors. (1) The FDA files the BLA, 0.9604, published: 98 of 2,475 applications received a refuse-to-file letter, 4.0% (Chahal HS, Mukherjee S, Sigelman DW, Temple R, JAMA Intern Med 2021, doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.8866, CDER applications 2008 to 2017). (3) The FDA reviews on the basis it agreed in June 2026, 0.60, judgement: its July 2026 minutes say a BLA 'based on the existing clinical data, is reasonable' (10-Q 0001104659-26-087815), but that reversed two written refusals of the same external-control evidence (December 2025 and March 2026, 10-K 0001104659-26-021898), and the prespecified 48-month analysis it will now read missed its primary endpoint, cUHDRS slowing 44% at p=0.144 (8-K 0001104659-26-111654). 0.9604 x 0.867 x 0.60 = 0.4996
column12: stated, since the asset is outside the gate model (not big pharma), and the third factor is the arguable one. How it is read: the June 2026 agreement makes the 36-month analysis (cUHDRS slowing 75%, p=0.003, 10-K) the basis of review, so the published filed rate applies only if the FDA holds to it; the case for holding is that the agreement is written, follows a Type A and a Type B meeting and names 36 months as the regulatory anchor, and that TFC still slowed 61% at 48 months; the case against is that the reviewing office rejected this evidence twice, the 48-month primary analysis was prespecified under a protocol submitted to the FDA, and the treated arm is 12 to 17 patients against a registry control. Held at 0.75 the probability is 0.6245, worth +$1.68 a share on the engine's share count; at a third, one written position in three, 0.2776, worth -$2.99

column11: analogue, filed and published: the share of eligible patients the US system operates on each year for an established elective brain operation. uniQure on refractory mesial temporal lobe epilepsy: 'Surgical treatment for refractory patients is lobectomy or laser tissue ablation but only approximately 1% of eligible patients undergo surgery annually' (FY2025 10-K, 0001104659-26-021898). Englot DJ et al., Epilepsy surgery trends in the United States, 1990-2008, Neurology 2012;78:1200-1206 (doi:10.1212/WNL.0b013e318250d7ea, PMID 22442428): '100,000 to 300,000 patients with intractable epilepsy in the United States were potential candidates for surgical treatment' and 'only 1,500 underwent surgery that year' (1990), 0.5% to 1.5%. Cross-check on capacity: Willis AW et al., Neurology 2014;82:163-171 (doi:10.1212/WNL.0000000000000017): 'approximately 1% (n = 8,420)' of 665,765 Medicare beneficiaries with Parkinson disease were treated with deep brain stimulation over 2007 to 2009, about 2,800 operations a year in that population alone, so this build's peak of about 240 procedures a year is under a tenth of one stereotactic procedure's Medicare volume
column12: the rate already carries what keeps a patient from an elective brain operation: referral, willingness and the surgical slots of a working system. The case for higher: Huntington's disease is fatal and AMT-130 would be its first disease-modifying therapy, where epilepsy and Parkinson disease have drugs that work for many. The case for lower: deep brain stimulation reached about 1% of elderly Parkinson patients over three years, about a third of this a year; an accelerated approval on a 12 to 17 patient study may hold neurologists back; and each AMT-130 operation needs a long MRI-guided infusion at a centre trained to give it
